concepts.objective: Identify changes in the population, measurement or target-generating process and distinguish within-environment performance from evidence about deployment.
Distinguish prediction from intervention targets and explain why neither predictive strength nor a causal label alone guarantees robustness.
Compare conditional relationships across environments and state the mechanism and support assumptions needed for a scoped invariance argument, without treating stability as causal proof.
Design external-environment checks for prediction and generation, including content preservation, failure monitoring and abstention when evidence does not cover the intended use.

sources.citation: Peters, Jonas; Janzing, Dominik; Schölkopf, Bernhard. Elements of Causal Inference: Foundations and Learning Algorithms. MIT Press, 2017.

claims.proposition: A relationship useful for prediction in observed environments need not apply in a new environment whose generating processes or support differ.

source_refs.locator: Section 8.3, Domain Adaptation, environments and equation (8.7)

claims.proposition: The most informative observational predictor need not be an effective intervention target, because prediction and changing the target are different tasks.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3, Example 6.10, Predictors and intervention targets

claims.proposition: Under a causal model, changes to other mechanisms can leave the target mechanism invariant. Domain generalization additionally assumes that the relevant conditional relationship persists in the test environment and has adequate support; stability can also occur for non-parent predictor sets.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.6, equation (6.7); Section 8.3, equation (8.7), discussion of non-parent sets and overlapping supports

claims.proposition: Evidence from multiple environments is interpreted under assumptions about which mechanisms change. Hidden variables and previously unexamined mechanism changes can invalidate an invariance argument.

source_refs.locator: Section 8.3, equation (8.7) assumptions; Section 9.5.6, restrictions on hidden variables and environment interventions

claims.proposition: Reference counts and assessment cases in this pack are authored teaching data. Interactive experiment outcomes are deterministically recomputed from the released model and learner settings. Ratios, differences and weighted sums use declared denominators and target weights. Generation fidelity and withholding criteria are declared teaching-model rules, not empirical guarantees or textbook claims about a particular generator.

resources.text: A warehouse wants an assistant to predict whether a parcel is damaged. The assistant can read a warehouse label or a recorded parcel-damage flag: a yes/no finding from a photograph. At the first warehouse, the label often matches the checking answer. Another warehouse may label parcels differently or take photographs that make damage harder to record.
Worked example

The assistant predicts whether a parcel is damaged. A reference is a separate answer used to check the prediction. Here it is a preset checking answer for whether the parcel is damaged, set by the teaching model before any measurement error. It is not a real clinical or inspection review.

The new warehouse may see different cases, use different warehouse labels or record the damage finding from the photograph less reliably. These are different changes. A fall in accuracy tells us that predictions are worse on the tested cases, not which change caused every error.

Test records from the intended warehouse, with suitable checking answers. Keep them separate from records used for training or tuning. In the practice, you will change how often the warehouse label matches the reference and test one fixed prediction rule.

Distribution shift means that the cases, measurements or process producing an outcome change between settings. An old test score describes the old setting; it does not guarantee performance after a change.
Splitting the first site's records again does not test new measurements at another site.
Name the setting that changed, then test predictions on cases representing that setting.

Records from the new site let the team check performance with the changed measurements. Use suitable checking answers and keep these records separate from training and tuning. Splitting the old records again can miss those measurement errors.
Where did the test records come from? Check whether they include the new measurements.
Which records contain the conditions the assistant will now face?
An assistant predicts whether a parcel is damaged. It was tested at one warehouse, but a second warehouse records images differently. How should the team test it at the second site?

Records from the new site let the team check performance with the changed measurements. Use suitable checking answers and keep these records separate from training and tuning. Splitting the old records again can miss those measurement errors.
Recording settings and case mix both changed, so these tests do not show how much each contributed to the lower accuracy.
Read the new result and list both changes. The comparison does not hold one fixed while testing the other.
Could these tests separate the effects of the recording settings from those of the case mix?
A parcel-damage predictor scored 90% at its original warehouse. A second warehouse changes both camera settings and parcel mix. Its new test score is 70%. What can we conclude from these tests?
Recording settings and case mix both changed, so these tests do not show how much each contributed to the lower accuracy.
The warehouse label often matches whether a parcel is damaged. Suppose we edit only that recorded marker. Could the assistant's prediction change while the parcel's condition stays the same?
Worked example

The warehouse label is a clue, sometimes called a cue. It can be useful because different kinds of cases arrive at different warehouses. Relabelling a recorded input is not an action that changes the parcel's condition. Prediction and changing an outcome are different tasks.

In the practice, compare the same case number before and after the marker edit. Its checking answer and recorded parcel-damage flag stay fixed. If the prediction changes, you have shown dependence on the marker. You have not shown that the marker caused or treated the underlying condition.

A causal explanation asks which processes produce the outcome and the recorded inputs. It can explain why a site shortcut may fail when those processes change. Other inputs still need checking: a feature proposed as a cause can be measured poorly or used for kinds of cases that have not been tested.

A shortcut is an input that predicts well in one setting because it is associated with the answer there. That does not mean changing the input changes the underlying outcome. A plausible causal feature also needs reliable measurement and new-setting checks.
Changing a prediction is not the same as changing the condition being predicted.
Ask what changed: the recorded input, the assistant's answer, or the underlying condition.
Changing only the recorded marker changed the prediction while the underlying condition stayed fixed. The other inputs still need testing.
Which part of the case did the edit change, and which part stayed fixed?
Separate the input, the prediction and the condition being described.
The assistant reads the warehouse label. We edit only that recorded marker; the parcel's condition stays fixed. Its prediction changes. What have we learned?
Changing only the recorded marker changed the prediction while the underlying condition stayed fixed. The other inputs still need testing.
The assumed causal link does not fix an inaccurate thickness measurement. Check the predictions for the new parcels and the process producing damage.
Which value reaches the assistant: the feature itself or the device's recorded measurement?
The assistant receives a measured value, not direct access to the proposed cause.
The teaching model assumes thicker cardboard reduces crushing damage. A new camera records thickness poorly. Does the causal role of thickness guarantee reliable damage predictions?
The assumed causal link does not fix an inaccurate thickness measurement. Check the predictions for the new parcels and the process producing damage.

The assistant now reads the recorded parcel-damage flag instead of the warehouse label. Ignoring the marker avoids that shortcut. But what happens if the recorded parcel-damage flag is recorded incorrectly more often?
Worked example

The image-reading rule copies the recorded parcel-damage flag. The teaching model first sets the checking answer and then sometimes records the opposite finding. This measurement is not a feature established to cause the target. Reading it is not direct access to truth.

A rule that ignores the site marker can stay unchanged when only the marker changes. It may still fail when its own measured input becomes less reliable. A causal account helps identify the processes assumed to stay fixed and distinguish changes that test different assumptions.

The same overall accuracy can hide different errors in different groups. A conditional comparison checks outcomes for cases with the same relevant measured features, over values represented in both settings. The range represented is called support. Reference-group error rates shown in this exercise are useful error checks, not a direct test of that outcome-given-features relationship or a unique causal graph.

An invariant relationship stays the same across the settings compared. Using it elsewhere assumes the relevant outcome process, measurements and range of cases remain suitable. Stable results are limited evidence, not proof of a cause or a guarantee for every new setting.
Stable scores under a marker change do not validate a new measurement process or an unseen kind of case.
Say what was held fixed, what changed and which changes still need testing.

The similar damage rates support stability for cardboard parcels with the same recorded finding at the tested warehouses. They do not check padded bags or establish a cause. A new warehouse may also change the process producing damage.
Does the conclusion include cases that none of the three sites tested?
Which kinds of cases did the teams actually compare?
Three warehouses compare cardboard parcels with the same recorded damage finding. They see similar damage rates. Padded bags were not tested. What does this support?

The similar damage rates support stability for cardboard parcels with the same recorded finding at the tested warehouses. They do not check padded bags or establish a cause. A new warehouse may also change the process producing damage.
An overall score mixes groups. Compare similar cases within those groups and check that there is enough data to judge uncertainty. A matching average alone does not do this.
How do the reported errors differ within the groups? Consider that alongside the overall score.
Could different group errors combine into the same overall score?

Two warehouses both report 85% accuracy. At the second, errors are higher for fragile parcels, and the parcel mix differs. Does the shared overall score show that performance stayed stable for similar parcels?
An overall score mixes groups. Compare similar cases within those groups and check that there is enough data to judge uncertainty. A matching average alone does not do this.

So far the assistant has predicted whether a parcel is damaged. Now it must write a short report from the recorded finding and its context. Some records do not contain the required context. Should it fill the gap or leave the report for review?
Worked example

The source is the recorded parcel-damage flag plus the context, if available. A draft that reverses a recorded finding fails source fidelity. A faithful copy can still preserve a wrong measurement, so comparing with the source is different from checking with the independent reference.

Complete every report writes a full draft and fills missing context with an unsupported detail. Preserve source facts copies available facts and withholds a full report when required context is absent. These are fixed teaching templates, not an LLM. Changing the report rule does not repair the input measurement.

Compare unsupported additions and full-report coverage over all cases. Also count source-supported reports among those issued. Withholding can reduce unsupported additions while leaving fewer cases with reports. If none are issued, fidelity among issued reports is undefined, not perfect. Withholding an unsupported claim, or abstaining, needs a clear review path and does not verify the missing fact.

Generation produces an output such as a report. Source fidelity means keeping the facts actually recorded without inventing details. It is not proof that the source is true. Coverage is the share of cases receiving a full report.
Fluent wording does not prevent invented facts, and copying the source can preserve a mistake. A withheld report has not supplied a correct answer.
Check prediction accuracy, source fidelity and coverage separately; make unsupported cases visible for review.
The draft contradicts its source. Source fidelity checks recorded meaning; it does not establish whether that source itself is correct.
Does the draft make the same factual claim as the source?
Compare the findings stated in the source and the draft.
Now the assistant writes a report. The source says 'no damage recorded', but the fluent draft says 'damage recorded'. Which check does the draft fail?
The draft contradicts its source. Source fidelity checks recorded meaning; it does not establish whether that source itself is correct.
Flag the missing fact and untested setup for review. Withholding a claim does not verify the missing fact. Evidence is still needed before extending use to these cases.
An old score and a confident draft cannot supply the missing source fact.
Is the needed fact actually recorded, and was this setup tested?
A new warehouse's record lacks a fact required for a full report. Its recording method has not been evaluated. What should the assistant do?
Flag the missing fact and untested setup for review. Withholding a claim does not verify the missing fact. Evidence is still needed before extending use to these cases.
